records.query: Summarize the procedures and safety requirements for removing, packaging, and handling wet and dry batteries from vehicles; mention hazard precautions as well.
records.reference: Wet batteries (except nickel, iron-alkaline) must be removed from vehicles and reported as excess, kept charged, and maintained in a charged condition while awaiting disposal instructions. Dry batteries should be space packaged and packed in accordance with Specification PPP-B-140, with vent holes sealed. Battery posts must be protected using plastic caps or tape conforming to Specification SAE AMS-T-22085. Wet batteries may remain installed in vehicles during military aircraft transport if protected against short circuits by disconnecting and securing cables away from terminals, and properly secured to prevent acid leakage. Dry batteries pose no special hazard and may be installed in the vehicle or shipped with OVE without additional precautions. Wet batteries received with vehicles may be used until the first exercise is completed, after which they must be transferred to a battery room, kept charged, and either shipped or replaced with dry batteries. Dry batteries, whether received charged or not, can be stored in the vehicle’s battery carrier, though indoor storage is preferred, and their vent holes must be sealed until activation. Cable terminals should be greased and taped according to military specifications, and dry batteries must not be activated unless no serviceable wet battery is available. Hazard precautions include preventing acid leakage and short circuits for wet batteries, and ensuring proper handling and activation procedures for dry batteries to avoid chemical exposure.
records.answer:
Summary of battery removal, packaging, handling and hazard precautions (sources: TO 36-1-191 vehicle storage/shipment; TO 1-1-691 battery electrolyte handling):

REMOVAL / DISCONNECT
- Clean batteries, cables and battery boxes with a solution of one pound of soda ash (A-A-59563) per gallon of water (TO 36-1-191, Table 8-2, Item 2a, AV vehicles, Level A).
- Disconnect cables, removing the ground cable first, and secure the ends to the battery support with tape conforming to SAE AMS-T-22085 (Item 2b).

WET (ELECTROLYTE-FILLED) BATTERIES
- Wet batteries removed from vehicles are reported to the appropriate property class as excess, requesting disposition instructions, and must be kept in a charged condition while awaiting disposition (P5097).
- Wet batteries may remain in vehicles for Level B and C storage; under Level A outside storage they may remain for exercise until no longer capable of recharging. Wet type batteries in closed cabs/bodies should be removed or replaced with dry charged batteries when reprocessing Level B storage (P5099).
- Wet batteries received with vehicles may be used until completion of the first exercise, then moved to a battery room and kept charged until shipped or replaced with a dry battery (P5154).
- Nickel-iron-alkaline batteries: confirm electrolyte is at the recommended level and filler caps are closed; discharge at normal rate to 0.5 V per cell and short-circuit each tray leaving wires connected during storage (P5099).

DRY BATTERIES
- Dry batteries are secured in vehicle battery carriers; vent holes in filler caps are plugged or sealed (P5097, P5099, P5154).
- Vent holes remain sealed until the battery is activated for shipment. No dry battery is activated until a check confirms a serviceable wet battery is available; the storage officer ensures enough electrolyte is on hand (P5154).
- Dry batteries offer no special hazard for air shipment and may be installed in the battery carrier or placed with OVE (P5157).

PACKAGING AND SHIPPING
- Dry batteries are packaged and packed per Specification PPP-B-140 (overseas requirements) (P5097).
- Electrolyte is packaged and packed per O-S-801 and stowed so it can be easily removed at ports when required by maritime regulations; packaged batteries and electrolyte are stowed with other OVE (P5097).
- Battery posts are covered with plastic caps or tape conforming to SAE AMS-T-22085 (P5097, P5099).
- For nickel-iron batteries, connector cables are preserved and packaged per MIL-STD-2073-1 and secured in the battery compartment or stored with the removed battery; batteries may be received discharged, dumped of electrolyte and short-circuited (P5100).
- Wet charged lead-acid batteries shipped in the vehicle battery carrier are covered with waterproofed protective paper (PPP-B-1055) extending down the sides and ends at least 6 inches, secured with AMS-T-22085 tape; shrouding is at the discretion of the responsible officer (P5100).
- Military airlift: vehicles may fly with a wet battery installed only if fully protected against short circuits (cables removed, ends kept away from terminals) and secured so acid leakage cannot occur. Wet batteries are packed per AFMAN 24-204(I)P. Electrolyte is packed per AFMAN 24-204(I)P and attached to the vehicle under the hood for air or sea shipment. Hazardous materials are not to be stripped for airlift or placed in consolidation containers. Obtain certification through the local Hazardous Materiel Certifier (LRS Distribution Flight) (P5157).

HAZARD PRECAUTIONS
- WARNING (TO 36-1-191): Electrolyte is highly toxic to skin, eyes and respiratory tract. Avoid all contact. Skin and eye protection and vapor control are required. Have the operation reviewed by the local Bioenvironmental Engineer. Failure to comply could result in injury to, or death of, personnel or long-term health hazards (P5097).
- WARNING (TO 36-1-191): When working around batteries, always wear eye protection (face shield), acid-resistant rubber apron and gloves (P5095).
- WARNING (TO 1-1-691): When handling electrolytes, wear chemical splash-proof goggles and chemical-resistant rubber gloves and aprons. If electrolyte contacts skin or eyes, flood the area immediately with water and report to the Base Medical Facility. An emergency shower and eye wash station are required where electrolyte work is performed (P2966).
- Electrolyte (sulfuric acid or potassium hydroxide) severely corrodes metal structures. Do not drip electrolyte on aircraft/equipment or let contaminated gloves, rags or sponges touch structures; place contaminated items in a leak-proof plastic container before removing them from the area. Remove any battery box holding spilled electrolyte before cleaning it, and clean spills as soon as detected (P2966).
- Neutralize spills: 10% by weight sodium bicarbonate solution for sulfuric acid (lead-acid); 3% by weight boric acid or monobasic sodium phosphate for potassium hydroxide (nickel-cadmium). Use litmus paper to detect acid (blue turns red) or alkaline (red turns blue) spills (P2966).
- Isopropyl alcohol (TT-I-735) used in the litmus solution is highly flammable; use only in a well-ventilated area away from ignition sources (P2966).
- Battery compartments and adjacent areas are corroded by electrolyte leakage; include them in battery compartment inspection and maintenance (P2859).

input.answer:
Summary of battery removal, packaging, handling and hazard precautions (sources: TO 36-1-191 vehicle storage/shipment, TO 1-1-691 and TO 1-1-700 battery/electrolyte handling):

REMOVAL / DISCONNECT
- Clean batteries, cables and battery boxes with a solution of one pound of soda ash (A-A-59563) per gallon of water (Table 8-2, Item 2a, AV vehicles, Level A).
- Disconnect cables, removing the ground cable first, and secure the ends to the battery support with tape conforming to SAE AMS-T-22085 (Item 2b).
- Battery cables are disconnected only on NMCS vehicles where electrical shorts or excessive voltage drop/current drain are possible; batteries are removed from NMCS vehicles subject to climatic extremes (P5149).

WET (LEAD-ACID / ELECTROLYTE-FILLED) BATTERIES
- Wet batteries removed from vehicles are reported to the appropriate property class as excess, requesting disposition instructions, and must be maintained in a charged condition while awaiting disposition (P5097).
- Wet batteries may remain in vehicles for Levels B and C storage; under Level A outside storage they may remain for exercise until no longer capable of recharging. Wet lead-acid batteries are kept fully charged in the vehicle battery box or battery room (P5099, P5154).
- Wet batteries may be used until completion of the first exercise, then moved to a battery room and kept charged until shipped or replaced with a dry battery (P5154).
- Nickel-iron-alkaline batteries: confirm electrolyte is at recommended level and filler caps closed; discharge at normal rate to 0.5 V per cell, and short-circuit each tray leaving wires connected during storage (P5099).

DRY BATTERIES
- Dry batteries are secured in vehicle battery carriers; vent holes in filler caps are plugged or sealed (P5097, P5099, P5154).
- Vent holes stay sealed until the battery is activated for shipment. No dry battery is activated until a check confirms a serviceable wet battery is available; the storage officer ensures enough electrolyte is on hand (P5154).
- Dry batteries offer no special hazard for air shipment and may be installed in the battery carrier or placed with OVE (P5157).

PACKAGING AND SHIPPING
- Dry batteries: packaged and packed per Specification PPP-B-140 (overseas requirements); electrolyte packed per O-S-801 (P5097, P5099).
- Electrolyte: packaged and packed per O-S-801 and stowed so it can be easily removed at ports when required by maritime regulations; packaged batteries and electrolyte are stowed with other OVE (P5097).
- Battery posts are covered with plastic caps or tape conforming to SAE AMS-T-22085 (P5097, P5099).
- Connector cables are preserved and packaged per MIL-STD-2073-1 and secured in the battery compartment or stored with the removed battery (P5100).
- Wet batteries shipped in the vehicle battery carrier are covered with waterproofed protective paper (PPP-B-1055) extending down the sides and ends at least 6 inches, secured with AMS-T-22085 tape; wet charged lead-acid batteries may be maintained charged for shipment or use (P5100).
- Military airlift: vehicles may fly with a wet battery installed only if fully protected against short circuits (cables removed, ends kept away from terminals) and secured so acid leakage cannot occur. Wet batteries are packed per AFMAN 24-204(I)P. Electrolyte is packed per AFMAN 24-204(I)P and attached to the vehicle under the hood for air or sea shipment (P5157). Hazardous materials are not to be stripped for airlift or put into consolidation containers.
- Coordinate hazardous-material certification through the local LRS/Hazardous Materiel Certifier (P5157).

HAZARD PRECAUTIONS
- WARNING (TO 36-1-191): Electrolyte is highly toxic to skin, eyes and respiratory tract. Avoid all contact. Skin and eye protection and vapor control are required. Have the operation reviewed by the local Bioenvironmental Engineer. Failure to comply could result in injury to, or death of, personnel or long-term health hazards (P5097).
- WARNING (TO 36-1-191): When working around batteries, always wear eye protection (face shield), acid-resistant rubber apron and gloves (P4949 section context; Table 8-2 Item 2 on P3? see P5095).
- WARNING (TO 1-1-691): When handling electrolytes, wear chemical splash-proof goggles and chemical-resistant rubber gloves and aprons. If electrolyte contacts skin or eyes, flood the area immediately with water and report to the Base Medical Facility. An emergency shower and eye wash station are required where electrolyte work is performed (P2966).
- Electrolyte (sulfuric acid or potassium hydroxide) severely corrodes metal structures. Do not drip electrolyte on aircraft/equipment or let contaminated gloves, rags or sponges touch structures; place contaminated items in a leak-proof plastic container before removing them from the area. Remove any battery box holding spilled electrolyte before cleaning it, and clean spills as soon as detected (P2966).
- Neutralize spills: 10% by weight sodium bicarbonate solution for sulfuric acid (lead-acid); 3% by weight boric acid or monobasic sodium phosphate for potassium hydroxide (nickel-cadmium). Use litmus paper to detect acid (blue turns red) or alkaline (red turns blue) spills (P2966).
- Isopropyl alcohol (TT-I-735) used in litmus solution is highly flammable; use only in a well-ventilated area away from ignition sources (P2966).
- Never pour water into acid; pour acid into water, as excess heat is generated. Use only in well-ventilated areas with rubber gloves, safety goggles with face shield, impervious boots, apron and coveralls (P3447, TO 1-1-700).
- Do not expose batteries to acid or acid vapors; electrolyte is extremely corrosive (P3254).
- Personnel working near highly toxic chemicals should be familiar with resuscitation methods; obtain information from base medical services (P4949).

records.query: List the processes in included in the Equipment Painting and list the precautions to be considered during surface painting.
records.reference: Equipment painting includes cleaning surfaces with degreasing solvents (MIL-PRF-680, Type II) and isopropyl alcohol (TT-I-735) to remove oil, grease, rust, and dirt; sanding glossy areas and removing rust by wire brushing; priming bare spots; and applying two coats of paint, allowing each coat to dry. Precautions include using PPE (eye, skin, and respiratory protection), ensuring adequate ventilation, avoiding contact with flammable and hazardous chemicals, following OSHA safety color coding, and not painting transparent shields. Items must be painted with materials that are not affected by fluids or cleaning solutions used in the machines.
records.answer:
Processes in Equipment Painting (TO 34-1-3, para. 2): The term "painting" covers any refinishing of machinery or equipment, from touch-up of the existing finish to complete repainting. Related processes covered are: complete repainting (surfaces restored to original color when possible), finish touch-up (extent determined by the using agency), surface preparation for previously painted machinery, and safety color coding of machines (red, yellow, orange, green, blue, magenta/purple, black/white or yellow per ANSI Z535.1 / AFMAN 91-203). Repainting new machines solely to match shop color schemes is not authorized.

Precautions for surface painting:
- A chemically clean surface is necessary for paint adhesion; a thin film of oil can prevent adhesion and slow drying. Surfaces must be clean, dry, and free from dust, grease, oil, rust, and dirt.
- Glossy surfaces should be sanded to dull the gloss. WARNING: sanding operations are hazardous to the eyes; eye protection is required.
- Remove all rust and scale by scraping or wire brushing.
- Degrease first with solvent MIL-PRF-680, Type II (or other approved solvent) to remove visible oil/grease, then clean with isopropyl alcohol, TT-I-735, until grease free. Degreasing solvent is flammable and hazardous; use adequate ventilation, wear skin and eye protection, and do not ingest. Isopropyl alcohol is flammable; keep away from heat, sparks and flame; use in a well-ventilated area; half-mask respirator required in poorly ventilated areas.
- Sand bare spots to a feather edge and spot prime with lacquer-proof primer. Machines will not be operated during painting. Allow each coat to dry thoroughly before the next (two coats in the required color).
- Use only paint materials not affected by any fluids or cleaning solutions used on the machine.
- Transparent shields should not be painted; non-hazardous fixed guards need not be painted.

General surface preparation (TO 1-1-8, Ch. 3): WARNING – refer to PPE table for paint preparation; provide adequate ventilation when using solvents, avoid prolonged breathing of vapors and skin contact, use protective gloves and eye protection. Surface preparation is the most important factor for paint adherence; surfaces must be thoroughly prepared before recoating. General aircraft/equipment painting safety (TO 1-1-8, Ch. 5): wear approved respiratory protection and protective clothing, wash hands before eating, and spray only in areas approved by Fire, Safety, and Bioenvironmental Engineering.

records.query: What are the procedures for installing, removing, and requisitioning vehicle markings, including reflective tape?
records.reference: Vehicle markings, including reflective tape, are installed by cleaning the surface, removing the liner, positioning the tape, and applying firm pressure. For removal, pressure-sensitive tape can be softened with heat and isopropyl alcohol (TT-I-735), while older tape requires paint remover (TT-R-2918) or 3M decal remover disks. Markings can be requisitioned through DLA Document Services Online. If decals are unavailable and safety is impacted, stenciling is permitted. Reflectors follow drawing B161059, mounted 24–60 inches above the ground, visible at 100 feet. Install tape according to the steps; damaged areas may be patched.
records.answer:
Based on TO 36-1-191 (Vehicle Management markings):

INSTALLATION OF REFLECTORIZED TAPE (para 2.88):
a. Clean the vehicle surface before applying the marking.
b. Remove the liner film down.
c. Position the emblem on the clean surface and tack it in place with thumb pressure.
d. Start in the center and use hard overlapping strokes of a low-friction plastic squeegee.
e. Re-squeegee the edges using very firm strokes.
f. Apply clean sealer to the edges of the tape.
g. Repairs to damaged areas can be made without stripping the original tape: clean the damaged area and apply new tape over the affected area.

REMOVAL OF REFLECTORIZED TAPE (para 2.89):
WARNING: Lacquer thinner, kylol, and isopropyl alcohol are flammable and toxic. Good general ventilation is normally adequate. Skin and eye protection is required. Avoid all sources of ignition. Failure to comply could result in injury to, or death of, personnel or long-term health hazards.
- 2.89.1 Routine removal: Soften pressure-sensitive tape with heat (heat lamp, heat gun, steam, etc.); soften adhesive residue with rags soaked in isopropyl alcohol (TT-1-735) and scrape away with a plastic scraper or putty knife.
- 2.89.2 Removing old tape: For tape applied for several years, mask off the area and brush paint remover (TT-R-2918, Type) over the tape. Apply several times at short intervals, removing residue with a plastic scraper or bevel-edge putty knife between applications. Paint remover may damage the underlying paint, requiring cleaning and touch-up painting.
- 2.89.3 Alternative: A 4 or 6 inch stripe, molding and decal remover disk (3M) removes tape without damaging the paint. Disks: NSN 5130-01-390-9503 (4 inch) and NSN 5130-01-390-9504 (6 inch); drill adapter NSN 5130-01-391-2095.
- NOTE: The solvents above are flammable and toxic; take all safety precautions.

REQUISITIONING MARKINGS (para 2.90):
All markings in this chapter are requisitioned through DLA Document Services. Submit requests via the Document Services Online (DSO) website; once an account is created, orders are processed through the Travis Plant. DLA Document Services: (707) 424-0770 / (707) 424-4537, DSN 837.
NOTE: If decals are not immediately available and the equipment hampers mission capability or presents a safety hazard unmarked, appropriate markings may be stenciled on the vehicle or equipment before decals are received.

RELATED MARKING REQUIREMENTS: Markings are to be applied with reflectorized tape and die-cut letters/numbers per ASTM D4956, Class 3, Type 1 (para 2.36). Upon transfer within the USAF, organization markings are removed; upon transfer to DRMS/AFSVS, AF markings and USAF registration numbers are obliterated or removed (data plates are not removed) (para 2.34). WRM triangle markings are removed when a vehicle leaves WRM status, but not when a WRM asset ships to a contingency area (para 2.87).

Note: The pages do not give a separate installation procedure for non-tape decals; the tape procedure above is the documented installation method.

records.query: What caution is taken into consideration while using high-pressure wash equipment, and explain the function of the portable, 45-gallon, foam-generating cleaning unit?
records.reference: When using high-pressure wash equipment, caution must be taken to ensure it is never used on aircraft landing gear and components, wheels, and brakes, as it can force lubricants out of bearings and attachment points, causing corrosion and wear problems. The function of the portable, 45-gallon, foam-generating cleaning unit is to dispense foam. This cleaning unit is a simplified, portable, pressure-operated, foam-dispensing system that uses the available air supply as its power source to force cleaning solution into the hose and create foam.
records.answer:
Caution with high-pressure wash equipment: Equipment developing more than 175 lbf/in² (PSI) nozzle pressure must NOT be used to apply cleaning compounds unless specifically authorized by the equipment System Program Manager (SPM); failure could damage or destroy equipment or cause loss of mission effectiveness. High-pressure wash equipment must never be used on components, wheels, and brakes, as it can force lubricants out of bearings and attach points and cause corrosion and wear. Where approved by the SPM, use only authorized cleaners, 40-degree flat fan spray nozzles, and maintain a nozzle standoff distance of at least 12 inches (never less). Also, high-pressure spray nozzles should not be used to apply cleaning compounds, which should be applied with a low-pressure soap nozzle, since high pressure can entrap compounds in enclosed areas and cause corrosion (TO 1-1-691).

Portable 45-gallon foam-generating cleaning unit: It is a simplified, portable, pressure-operated foam-dispensing system. records.query: Define CSO and list down the activities performed in the presence of CSS.
records.reference: Concurrent Servicing Operations (CSO) are the simultaneous servicing of fuel and other aircraft operations such as munitions loading/unloading, aircraft reconfiguration, and aircraft -6 TO inspections. The Chief Servicing Supervisor (CSS) is responsible for on-site supervision of all aspects of concurrent fuel servicing operations. The CSS's activities include ensuring all non-essential personnel and equipment are cleared from the area, briefing team members on duties and emergency procedures, checking the status of the aircraft and its systems with the SCR, ensuring cabin crew have briefed passengers, directing and monitoring the positioning of support equipment and personnel, and having SPR/Vent monitors reposition aircraft wheel chocks as required.
records.answer:
CSO (Concurrent Servicing Operations): Per TO 00-25-172, CSO supporting Combat Sortie Generation (CSG) is the simultaneous fuel servicing and munitions/ammunition loading/unloading, aircraft reconfiguration, aircraft -6 TO inspections, and other aircraft servicing such as oil, nitrogen, and hydraulic fluid. Oxygen servicing will not be accomplished during fuel servicing. Simultaneous servicing with no munitions loading/unloading or aircraft reconfiguration is called just "Concurrent Servicing." (CSO supporting CSG was renamed ICT in a later release, with the same definition.)

Activities performed in the presence of the CSS (Chief Servicing Supervisor): The CSS is the on-site supervisor responsible for all aspects of fuel servicing, munitions/ammunition loading/unloading, aircraft reconfiguration, aircraft -6 TO inspections, and other aircraft servicing performed during CSOs. The key function requiring a CSS is refueling/defueling; if no refuel/defuel operations occur concurrently with other maintenance/munitions tasks, a CSS is not required. Activities requiring a CSS include:
1. Simultaneous fuel servicing with aircraft -6 and -6WC inspections (electrical "power-on" portions of -6 inspections are not authorized during concurrent munitions loading/unloading and fuel servicing).
2. Simultaneous fuel servicing with munitions/ammunition loading/unloading.
3. Simultaneous fuel servicing with aircraft reconfiguration.
4. Simultaneous fuel servicing and other aircraft servicing such as oil, nitrogen, and hydraulic fluid.
5. Simultaneous fuel servicing with loading/unloading of munitions, aircraft reconfiguration, aircraft -6 TO inspections, and other servicing (oil, nitrogen, hydraulic fluid).

Related CSS duties during concurrent servicing: the CSS wears a reflective vest with "CSS" on front and back, controls and monitors all concurrent servicing operations, and notifies the Fire Department at least 15 minutes before CSO begins (and the number of people aboard, if personnel remain on board). A CSS is not used for ICTs; an Aircraft Turnaround Supervisor (ATS) is used instead.

Note: The pages do not contain a single consolidated list of CSS activities; the list above is compiled from the CSO requirements in TO 00-25-172 and its checklists.

records.query: Outline the exception for taxiing within the 50-foot hot refueling safety zone, specifying the engine boundary rule and the mandatory fire protection assets that must be present.
records.reference: An exception allows part of a taxiing aircraft to pass within the 50-foot hot refueling safety zone, provided its operating engine(s) do not penetrate the 50-foot criteria. During this operation, one flightline fire extinguisher must be located within 100 feet of the aircraft, and one ARFF vehicle must be in standby posture.
records.answer:
Taxiing exception (TO 00-25-172, p. 49): Part of an aircraft may pass within 50 feet of a hot refueling operation, provided the operating engine(s) of the taxiing aircraft do not penetrate the 50-foot criteria. In other words, the engine boundary rule is that the running engines must stay outside the 50-foot hot refueling zone; only the non-engine portions of the aircraft may be within that distance. Note that the separation may not be reduced below 50 feet at existing parking areas, and the 50-foot criteria applies to the hot refueling area defined in the manual.

Fire protection: The manual does not state a separate, mandatory fire protection asset specifically for the taxiing exception. The fire protection requirements that apply to hot refueling (Table 3-1, item 3) are: one flightline fire extinguisher located within 100 feet of the aircraft, and one ARFF vehicle in standby posture, with positioning determined by the Installation Fire Chief. The Table 3-1 entries for multiple hot refueling and concurrent servicing carry the same requirements, and USAFE has additional requirements in a note at Paragraph 3.11, which was not reviewed.

Gap: The pages reviewed do not explicitly tie the taxiing exception to specific fire protection assets; the fire protection listed above is the general hot refueling requirement.
